summary: Thomas Dohmke, CEO of GitHub, sits down with Eugene Yan at the AI Engineer World's Fair to discuss the past, present, and future of GitHub Copilot. Dohmke traces Copilot's origins to 2020 during COVID lockdown, when GitHub engineers gained early access to OpenAI's Codex. The first breakthrough was seeing the model correctly place curly braces in JavaScript and write Python code. The team built the autocompletion feature entirely remotely, then shipped an internal staff ship preview that achieved an NPS of 72-73. After public release in mid-2021, telemetry showed Copilot wrote about 25% of code in enabled files, growing to roughly half over time. Dohmke explains GitHub's agile approach to AI strategy and the guiding philosophy of building AI for engineers rather than autonomous AI engineers. Ghost text autocompletion was designed to work around hallucinations while keeping developers in flow. The conversation turns to Copilot Workspace, which bridges GitHub issues to code implementation through specification, analysis, planning, and implementation steps with human interaction at every stage. Dohmke highlights how LLMs' multilingual capabilities democratize coding globally, enabling kids and adults to create in their native language. In the professional context, Copilot democratizes access to institutional knowledge, reducing anxiety for new employees. When asked to define an agent, Dohmke compares it to an AI dishwasher—fill it, let it run, take the output. He notes CI/CD and monitoring bots as existing autonomous agents. He criticizes current security tooling for adding to backlogs rather than fixing issues, expressing desire for agents that burn down security backlogs so developers can focus on creative, innovative work. Dohmke frames the current moment as another step function in software development—comparable to the PC, internet, open source, and mobile waves—encouraging developers to embrace their creativity and build new things.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Eugene Yan introduces Thomas Dohmke, CEO of GitHub, highlighting his career building developer tools and oversight of GitHub Copilot's launch.

sections.title: Copilot Origin Story
sections.summary: Dohmke recounts Copilot's 2020 origins during COVID lockdown: early access to OpenAI's Codex, the first aha moment with JavaScript and Python code generation, building autocompletion remotely, internal staff ship with NPS of 72-73, and telemetry showing 25% then ~50% of code generated.

sections.title: Integrating Copilot Across GitHub
sections.summary: Dohmke discusses GitHub's agile approach to AI strategy, the human-centric philosophy of building AI for engineers, ghost text as a way to handle hallucinations, and keeping developers in flow by eliminating browser-editor context switching.

sections.title: Copilot Workspace
sections.summary: Dohmke explains Copilot Workspace, which bridges GitHub issues to code implementation through specification, analysis, planning, and implementation steps with human interaction at each stage. He emphasizes assistive over autonomous agents and notes non-developers can use it for task sizing.

sections.title: Natural Language and Democratization
sections.summary: Dohmke discusses how LLMs enable coding in major human languages, democratizing access for kids and adults worldwide. In the professional context, Copilot democratizes access to institutional knowledge, reducing anxiety for new employees who would otherwise need to ask many questions.

sections.title: Defining Agents and the AI Dishwasher Analogy
sections.summary: Dohmke defines an agent as an AI dishwasher—fill it, let it do its thing, take the output. He cites CI/CD pipelines and monitoring bots as existing autonomous agents. He criticizes current security tooling for merely flagging issues rather than fixing them, adding to developer backlogs instead of reducing them.

sections.title: Desired Agents and Balancing Security vs Innovation
sections.summary: Dohmke expresses desire for agents that burn down security backlogs. He discusses the tension between security/compliance and innovation, noting leaders always want to go faster but must balance trust and speed. He highlights the need for new abstraction layers to manage the development lifecycle.

sections.title: Advice for Developers and Step-Function Framing
sections.summary: Dohmke frames the current AI moment as a step function comparable to the PC, internet, open source, and mobile waves. He encourages developers to embrace creativity and build new things, noting that as CEO he rarely codes and doesn't want to spend his limited coding time updating dependencies.
